title: Quick start
text: Goal: an NPC that talks when the player presses E. It takes about 5 minutes. Enable the plugin. Go to Edit → Plugins, search "Tag Dialogue", enable it and restart the editor. Create the UI. The first time the editor opens, a popup appears. Click Create Templates . - This creates ready-made dialogue widgets and sets them as the defaults. - You can do it later from Tools → Tag Dialogue → Create UI Templates , or by right-clicking a Content folder → Create Dialogue UI Templates . Create a dialogue. In the Content Browser: right-click → Tag Dialogue → Dialogue . Name it DA_Shopkeeper and open it. Write it. - A Start node and a first line ("Hello!") are already there. - Click the line and type its text in Details. - Right-click the graph → Add Line to add more, and wire the line's output into the next line's input. - Click Add option on a line to give the player choices. Add the component. Open your NPC Blueprint → Add Component → TDS Dialogue , then set Dialogue to DA_Shopkeeper . Start it. In the NPC (or player) Blueprint, when the player interacts, call Start Dialogue on the TDS Dialogue component. Pass the player pawn as Instigator . Play. - The dialogue widget appears. - Space , Enter or left click continues; Up/Down and 1–9 pick options. - When the conversation ends, input goes back to the game. Until you set up a UI, Print To Screen (on by default on the component) prints every line and option to the screen.

title: How it works: tags
text: Tag Dialogue stores the game's story state as Gameplay Tags. It does this in two ways: Send Tag (an event) Add Tag (memory) What it means "This just happened" "This is now true" Remembered? No. Listeners hear it once. Yes, until removed. Saved with the game. Example Door.Main.Knock Quest.FindKey , Item.Key.Picked All remembered tags together are called the tag state . Dialogue reads it for conditions, locked options and tasks. Your Blueprints read and write it with simple nodes: Send Tag, Add Tag, Remove Tag, Has Tag, Wait For Tag and Listen For Tag. Parent tags count. Having Quest.FindKey.Done also counts as having Quest.FindKey unless you ask for an exact match. Listening to Quest hears every Quest.* tag. Create your tags in Project Settings → Gameplay Tags as usual. Importing JSON adds missing tags for you.

title: The dialogue editor
text: Double-click a Dialogue asset to open it. Graph (left): the conversation. It flows left to right. Details (right): the selected node's settings. Toolbar: Arrange : lays the whole graph out as a tidy left-to-right tree. Undo works. Find box (Ctrl+F) Follow play toggle (see Live debugger ) Asset settings (click an empty spot in the graph): Setting What it does Default Speaker Name used by every line that has no speaker of its own. Default Portrait Portrait used by every line that has none. UI Style How this conversation is shown: UI.Dialogue.List , UI.Dialogue.Wheel , UI.Dialogue.Subtitle , or your own. Empty = the default widget. Working in the graph Adding nodes: right-click → Add Line / Option / Condition / Pick / End / Comment. Wires: drag from an output pin to an input pin. Actions on a wire: double-click any wire, or right-click it → Insert on this wire . See Actions . Comments: select nodes and press C to wrap them in a comment box. Copy and paste work as usual. Pasted nodes get new IDs. Pin colors and shapes. Inputs are tall bars on the left of a node and outputs are short bars on the right. A wire that leads nowhere ends the conversation. An End node does the same, but makes the ending visible.

title: Nodes
text: Start Where the conversation begins on a fresh talk. When a task is running, the NPC may start somewhere else instead (see Tasks ). Line Something a speaker says. Field What it does Speaker Who says it. Empty = the asset's Default Speaker. Portrait Image for the UI. Empty = the Default Portrait. Text The line. Supports text variables like {PlayerName} . Audio Voice clip. It plays on the NPC and stops when the next line starts. Once Only Play this line the first time only. Later talks skip it and go straight on; actions on its wire still run. Remembered per NPC and saved. Ignored on lines with options. On Enter Actions Actions that run the moment the line starts (e.g. open a door while the NPC speaks). A line either continues (one wire out) or asks (has options). Option What the player says. (Lines are what the NPC says.) Click Add option on a line, or right-click → Add Option and wire the line into it. Field What it does Text The player's words, short ("I need a sword."). Subtitle Shown on hover: the full sentence or a hint ("I need a blade strong enough for the road."). Required Tags The option is locked unless all these tags are in the tag state. Hide When Locked Hide a locked option instead of graying it out. After Closed What a closed option looks like: Gray Out or Hide (see Close Task). Instant Picking it doesn't show the player's line; the reply plays right away. Actions Run when the option is picked. Starts Task Picking it starts a task (see Tasks ). Condition Shows nothing. It checks the tag state and goes True or Else . Set Condition with the standard Gameplay Tag Query editor: All / Any / No Tags Match, and nested expressions. An empty condition is always true. Example: If Quest.Key.Done → "Thanks again!" / Else → "Have you seen my key?" Pick Shows nothing. Each time the conversation passes through, it takes one of its outputs. Use + / − on the node to add or remove outputs. Pick Mode Behavior Random A random output, never the same one twice in a row. In Order, Loop 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3… In Order, Stay On Last 1, 2, 3, 3, 3… (great for "first time / second time / every time after") Progress is remembered per NPC and saved. End Ends the conversation.

title: Actions (pills on wires)
text: Actions are small colored pills that sit on a wire. They run when the conversation passes along that wire. Double-click a wire to add one. Pill What it does SEND · Send Tag Broadcasts a tag once. Doors, quests and pickups listening for it react. ADD · Add Tag Adds a tag to the tag state (remembered and saved). REMOVE · Remove Tag Removes a tag from the tag state. WAIT · Wait For Tag Pauses the conversation until the tag is sent or added. The UI hides, the player goes and does it, and then the conversation continues from this wire. Pass If Already Added continues at once if the tag is already there. CLOSE · Close Task Closes an option for good (usually the one that gave a task). The option grays out or hides, and the NPC forgets the task. Put it on the "done" flow. Where they can go: the wire out of a line an option's wire a condition's True and Else wires a Pick's outputs a line's On Enter Your own actions: create a Blueprint subclass of TDS Action and override Execute . Context is the NPC that owns the dialogue. It then appears in the action dropdown.

title: Tasks (quests)
text: Any option can start a task. Tick Starts Task on the option and fill in the fields: Field Example Meaning Task Tag Quest.FindKey Added when the task starts. Means "running". Done Tag Quest.FindKey.Done Means "complete". Complete On Tags Item.Key.Picked The task completes when all of these have been sent or added, in any order. The plugin then adds and sends the Done Tag. Leave it empty to add the Done Tag yourself. Ask → line Played when the player talks again while the task is running ("Found it yet?"). Reward → line Played once , the first talk after completion ("You found it! Take this."). Done → line Played if the player picks the option again after the reward ("I already gave you one."). On the Option node, the Ask, Reward and Done pins are wired like any other output. What the NPC does on each talk: task not started → Start task running → Ask task complete → Reward (once) after reward → Start; picking the task option again → Done Already done before accepting. If the player picks the task option when its Complete On Tags already happened (they found the key first), the NPC goes straight to the Reward. Canceling a task. If you remove the Task Tag, the task is canceled and the NPC starts from the beginning again. Progress in Blueprint. Call Get Task Progress on the Tag Subsystem (e.g. "1 / 2" for a quest log) and Get Dialogue State on the component.

title: Text variables
text: Write {Name} in any line, speaker, option or subtitle. It's replaced when shown. "You have {Gold} gold, {PlayerName}." Kind Where Saved? Built in {PlayerName} is the Dialogue Hub's Player Display Name ("Me" by default). n/a Global On the Tag Subsystem, for every NPC. Yes Per NPC On the TDS Dialogue component (Text Variables map). These win over global ones. No Blueprint functions (the same set on the Tag Subsystem and on the component): Function What it does Set Text Variable Adds or updates. Returns whether it changed, the old value, and whether it was new. Add Text Variable Adds only. False if it already exists. Update Text Variable Changes only. False if it doesn't exist. Returns the old value. Remove Text Variable Removes. Returns the old value. Get Text Variable Reads one. Set Number Variable / Add To Number Variable / Get Number Variable Numbers, shown in the player's format (1,250). Add To takes negative amounts too. On Text Variable Changed (Tag Subsystem) fires for every change, which is handy for a HUD gold counter. Unknown names stay as written, so a typo shows up on screen instead of silently disappearing.

title: The TDS Dialogue component
text: Add it to anything that talks: NPCs, radios, notes, doors. It never decides when to talk; your Blueprint calls Start Dialogue. Settings Setting What it does Dialogue The conversation asset. UI Style Override Show this NPC differently from what the asset says (e.g. a radio uses UI.Dialogue.Subtitle ). Play Voice / Voice 2D / Voice Volume / Voice Attenuation Line audio. 2D is for narrators and radios; 3D comes from the actor. Save Id The name of this NPC's memory in saves. Empty = the actor's name, which is fine for NPCs placed in a level. Set it for spawned NPCs. Text Variables Per-NPC variables (see above). Barks / Bark Cooldown / Bark Min Time See Barks . Print To Screen Debug text on screen. Turn it off once you have a UI. Functions Function What it does Start Dialogue (Instigator) Starts talking. Pass the player pawn so the right player's UI shows it. Continue Next line (for lines without options). Select Option (Index) Picks an option. Use the Index from the option view. End Dialogue Stops now (e.g. the player walked away). Reset Dialogue Forgets this NPC's task progress and closed options. Close Option / Reopen Option / Is Option Closed Manual control over closed options. Get Dialogue State Not Started, Task Running, Task Done (reward waiting) or Task Rewarded. Handy for a "!" or "?" above the NPC's head. Is In Dialogue / Is Waiting For Tag State checks. Events: On Dialogue Started, On Line Started (line + options), On Waiting For Tag, On Dialogue Ended, On Bark, On Bark Ended. Async loading. Portraits and voices of the lines the player can reach next load in the background, so there are no hitches.

title: Barks
text: Barks are lines an NPC says on its own: "Nice weather." or "Hey, watch it!". No UI takes over and no input is locked. Create a normal Dialogue asset for the barks. Usually it's a Pick (Random) node into a few lines, optionally behind a Condition . On the TDS Dialogue component, set Barks to that asset. Call Bark (e.g. on overlap, on a timer, when hit). - Bark Override plays a different asset this time, e.g. a "hurt" set. - Ignore Cooldown skips the cooldown. - It returns false if the NPC is in a conversation, on cooldown, already barking, or has nothing to say. A bark plays from its start line through conditions, picks and Next wires. Each line stays up for its voice length, or for a time based on its text length (at least Bark Min Time ). Showing barks. Use any mix of these: Way How Subtitles (default) Project Settings → Tag Dialogue UI → Show Bark Subtitles is on by default. Nearby barks show as subtitles at the bottom of the screen. Set Bark Subtitle Widget to use your own (the templates create WBP_TDS_CinematicBark ). Above the head Add a TDS Bark Widget component to the NPC. It shows a speech bubble; Widget Class empty = a simple dark bubble. Your own widget just needs a TDS Bark Text or TDS Bark Subtitle inside. Max Distance hides far barks. Your own Bind On Bark on the component (one NPC) or on the Tag Subsystem (every NPC). Speaker colors (Project Settings → Tag Dialogue UI → Speaker Colors) color names in bark subtitles and dialogue text.

title: UI
text: How a conversation finds its widget NPC's UI Style Override → dialogue asset's UI Style → Default Widget Project Settings → Plugins → Tag Dialogue UI maps style tags to widgets: Default Widget : used when a style has no widget of its own. Style Widgets : style tag → widget. Add your own styles under UI.Dialogue in Gameplay Tags. A missing style falls back to its parent: UI.Dialogue.Wheel.Small → UI.Dialogue.Wheel → Default. Auto Show : creates and shows the widget when the player starts talking. Turn it off to show widgets yourself (Common UI stack, your own HUD). Built-in styles: UI.Dialogue.List , UI.Dialogue.Wheel and UI.Dialogue.Subtitle . Templates Create Templates makes five widgets and sets them as defaults: Widget Use WBP_TDS_Cinematic Default: speaker, line, option list. WBP_TDS_CinematicWheel Options on a wheel. WBP_TDS_CinematicSubtitle Subtitles only (radio, narrator). WBP_TDS_CinematicOption The option button used by the list. WBP_TDS_CinematicBark Bark subtitles. Open them and restyle freely. They're normal Widget Blueprints. Building your own widget with blocks Drop these into any Widget Blueprint. They find the conversation by themselves, with no Blueprint wiring needed. Block What it shows TDS Text Set Source to one of: Speaker, Line, Hovered Option, Hovered Option Subtitle or Player Name. Line mode has a typewriter, typing sounds, a speaker prefix, speaker colors and auto-advance. TDS Option List One entry per option. Entry Box Type picks the layout: Vertical, Horizontal, Wrap or Radial. Entry Class = your own button. TDS Option Wheel Options as a ring, with mouse and stick pointing. TDS Option Button The built-in entry. Make a child Blueprint and name widgets Button , Label , NumberText and SubtitleText ; they're filled for you. TDS Portrait The speaker's portrait. TDS Continue Prompt Visible only when the player can continue. Put your own icon or text inside; click to continue. TDS Bark Subtitle / TDS Bark Text Barks (see above). Fully custom UI You can skip the blocks entirely: Interface: implement TDS Dialogue View on any object and register it with Get Dialogue Hub → Register View . You get On Dialogue Opened, On Line Shown, On Options Shown, On Option Hovered, On Typing Changed, On Waiting For Tag, On Dialogue Closed and On Point Direction. Events: bind the Dialogue Hub 's events from any Blueprint (On Conversation Started, On Line Shown, and so on). Talking back: use the Session : Advance, Choose (or Choose Next Frame from button clicks), Hover, Hover Step, Choose Hovered, Choose By Number and End. Common UI If your project uses Common UI: TDS Dialogue Layer: drop it into your root layout and turn Auto Show off. TDS Common Dialogue Widget: a base class for the dialogue widget (Back ends the talk, and gamepad focus goes to the first option). TDS Common Option Button: an option entry with Common UI navigation. TDS Common Key Hint: "[A] Continue" hints with the right icon per device.

title: Input and controls
text: Project Settings → Tag Dialogue UI → Controls (works with any UI): Setting Default Confirm Keys (continue / choose highlighted) Space, Enter, Left Mouse, Gamepad A Previous / Next Keys Up / Down, D-pad Cancel Keys (walk out) Empty = the player can't leave mid-conversation Number Keys Choose On (1–9) Stick Points At Options On (wheel) Block Game Input Off Per style ( Input → Style Input ). Each UI style can treat input differently: Manage Input Mode Show Mouse Cursor Block Game Input Built In Controls UI.Dialogue.Subtitle comes preset to no mouse and no lock, so the player keeps walking while a radio talks. Turn Built In Controls off to drive the Session from your own Enhanced Input actions.

title: TDS Tag State component
text: This component makes an actor follow the tag state, so the world matches the story with no save code . Setting Example When A tag query, e.g. Any Tags Match: Item.Key.Picked Action Hide (hides it and turns off collision), Show (hidden until met), Destroy , or Events Only It checks on Begin Play, every time tags change, and after loading a save. On State Changed (Met) fires each time, so you can do anything else in Blueprint (play an animation, open a gate). Add several to one actor for several reactions. Examples: A key pickup with Hide when Item.Key.Picked . A gate blocker with Hide when Quest.FindKey.Done . A reward chest with Show when Reward.Sword . Prefer Hide over Destroy . A destroyed actor can't come back if the player loads an older save in the same session.

title: Blueprint nodes for tags
text: Usable from any Blueprint, with no setup: Node What it does Send Tag (+ Payload) Broadcasts once. The payload carries an Actor, a Number and a Text (e.g. who gave how many coins). Add Tag / Remove Tag Change the tag state. Has Tag (Exact Match) Reads the tag state. Wait For Tag Async node: fires On Received once when the tag is sent or added. Options: Exact Match, Pass If Already Added, and Timeout (fires On Timeout ). Listen For Tag Async node: fires On Received every time, until Stop Listening or the Blueprint is destroyed. Good for quest logs. On the Tag Subsystem (Get TDSTagSubsystem): Get Tag State / Set Tag State On Tag Sent / On Tag State Changed Watch Task Completion / Get Task Progress the text variable functions the save functions

title: Save and load
text: Tag Dialogue remembers: the tag state running tasks every NPC's memory: task progress, closed options, Once Only lines and Pick positions global text variables NPC memory lives in the subsystem, so NPCs in unloaded levels are saved too. Option A: built-in slot. This is the simplest. Save To Slot (Slot Name, User Index) writes Saved/SaveGames/<Slot>.sav . Load From Slot reads it back. NPCs already in the level update right away. Option B: your own save system. Capture Save Data returns one struct. Store it in your own Save Game, cloud save or database. Restore Save Data puts it back. New game: Reset All Dialogue State . On State Restored fires after restore, load or reset. Spawned NPCs: give each one a fixed Save Id on its TDS Dialogue component so its memory finds it again.

title: Import and export (JSON, CSV)
text: Right-click a Dialogue asset in the Content Browser: Command What it does Export Dialogue (JSON) / Import Dialogue (JSON) The whole dialogue: lines, options, actions, tasks and node positions. Export Texts (CSV) / Import Texts (CSV) Only Id, Kind, Speaker, Text, Subtitle , for writers and translators. Importing updates texts by Id and keeps the graph, pills and comments. Reimport Re-reads the .json the asset came from. Creating assets from JSON Drag one or many .json files into the Content Browser. Each becomes a Dialogue asset named after its file. Tags the project doesn't have yet are added automatically to Project Settings → Gameplay Tags. Files without node positions (hand-written or AI-written) are arranged automatically . Exported files keep their layout. Problems such as broken links or unknown action types are reported in one message after import. To write dialogues with AI, give the AI Writing Guide to any AI chat. It contains everything the AI needs: it asks you a few questions, then writes ready-to-import JSON. It's also the full reference for the JSON format.

title: Live debugger and search
text: Live debugger. Keep a dialogue open while you Play In Editor. The node each NPC is on glows green , and nodes already passed stay outlined. With Follow play on, the graph keeps the playing node in view. It works for barks too. Find (Ctrl+F). Searches line text, speakers, options, conditions, pills and comments. Enter jumps to the next match, and matches are outlined.

title: Demo level
text: Tools → Tag Dialogue → Open Demo Level (or Open Demo on the first-run popup) opens a small village. It shows: Blacksmith: a task with Ask / Reward / Done, a Once Only welcome and a random Pick for the reminder. Guard: a Condition, a locked option (needs the sword), a Once Only warning and {Gold} . Villagers: random barks that change after the quest. Radio: the Subtitle style with an In Order Pick. Key and gate: TDS Tag State components. The demo dialogues' JSON files are in the plugin's Docs/Demo folder.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Problem Fix Nothing shows on screen Run Create Templates, or set a Default Widget in Project Settings → Tag Dialogue UI. Check that Start Dialogue gets the player pawn as Instigator. The dialogue shows twice You use a TDS Dialogue Layer or your own widget and Auto Show is still on. Turn it off. Can't click options Turn on Manage Input Mode / Show Mouse Cursor for that style (Style Input). Player keeps walking during dialogue Turn on Block Game Input (globally, or per style). Barks don't show Check Show Bark Subtitles, the TDS Bark Widget's Max Distance, and that the NPC isn't in a conversation. Bark returns false on cooldown. Bark shows twice You have both a bubble and a full-screen subtitle listening. Keep one, or turn off Listen To All Barks on the extra subtitle. A spawned NPC forgets its task after loading Give it a fixed Save Id . {Name} shows literally The variable isn't set (or is misspelled). Names are exact. Reimport fails on an old asset Use Import Dialogue (JSON) once. After that Reimport remembers the file. Support: yahya@harcs.studio · Docs: yahyagames.github.io/TagDialogue-Docs

title: Writing with AI (JSON)
text: For the human: upload or paste this whole file into any AI chat (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini...), then say "Let's start". The AI asks about your story, shows you the dialogue as an easy-to-read story map for your OK, then writes the JSON you drag straight into Unreal. You decide the story; the AI handles the structure and tells you what the plugin can and can't do. For the AI: everything below is your instructions. Follow them for the whole conversation. 1. Your role You are the dialogue assistant for Tag Dialogue , an Unreal Engine 5 plugin. You do three jobs: Turn the user's story into dialogues : JSON files they import into Unreal (drag the .json into the Content Browser). Edit dialogues the user exports from Unreal (Export Dialogue (JSON)) and give them back ready to reimport. Answer questions about the plugin, using sections 7 and 9. If something isn't covered there, say you're not sure rather than inventing features. Who decides what The user owns the story. Characters, plot, quests, choices, outcomes and endings come from them. Don't invent major story points: new characters, twists, deaths, rewards or how a quest ends. If something is missing, ask, or offer 2–3 short ideas for the user to pick from. You own the structure. You turn their story into correct nodes, tags and JSON. You tell them what the plugin can and can't do (section 7). When an idea isn't possible as described, say so and propose the closest working way. You may write the wording. Write the actual lines and options in the voice the user wants: phrasing, small talk, bark variety. Stay inside their story. If they give exact lines, use them word for word. You lead the process Unless the user says otherwise, you drive the session: After every step, end with one clear next step , e.g. "Next: I'll write the guard's barks. Shall I?" Keep track of what's done and what's left (e.g. every NPC in their story). Propose the next item yourself instead of waiting. If the user changes direction, follow them. Two rules you never break Lines are what the NPC (or any speaker that isn't the player) says. Options are what the player says. Write them in the player's voice, in the first person: "I need a sword.", "Who are you?", "Goodbye." 2. Start of the conversation Greet the user in one sentence, then ask the setup questions below in one message , as a short numbered list. Keep it friendly and short, and skip anything they already answered. Story. What happens? Who is the player talking to, what do they want, and how can it end? Is there a quest: what must the player do, and what do they get? (No default. This must come from the user.) Characters. Who speaks? A name and one line of personality each. (No default. Ask, or offer ideas to choose from.) Tags. Do you already have Gameplay Tags for quests and items? Paste them if so. Otherwise I'll set up a naming pattern for you. [default: the pattern in section 4] What to make. A conversation with choices, barks (short random lines an NPC says on its own, no UI), or a radio/narrator (lines only, no choices)? [conversation] UI style. List (options in a list), Wheel (2–6 short options in a ring) or Subtitle (no choices)? [List] Variables. Does your game set any text variables, like {Gold} ? ( {PlayerName} always works.) [none besides {PlayerName}] Language and tone. [English, natural spoken game dialogue] If the user skips the technical questions (3–7), use the defaults in brackets and say which ones you used. Never fill in the story (1–2) yourself without asking. Remember the user's story, tags, characters and variables for the whole conversation, and reuse them in every new dialogue. 3. How you work: story map first, then JSON JSON is hard to read, so the user always sees the dialogue in plain form before getting the JSON. Step 1: Story map (for approval) Show the dialogue as a simple tree. NPC lines: Name: "text" Player options: ▸ You: "text" Invisible logic: in square brackets, in plain words Endings: → END Jumps: → (goes to: name of the moment) Example: [First visit only] Khalid: "Welcome to my forge, stranger. Mind the sparks." Khalid: "What can I do for you, {PlayerName}?" ▸ You: "I need a sword." [starts quest: find the key] Khalid: "Find my storeroom key and the blade is yours." → END ▸ You: "What is this place?" Khalid: "Stonebrook. A forge, a fountain, and a grumpy guard." → END ▸ You: "Goodbye." → END [While the quest is running, when you talk again: one at random] Khalid: "Any luck with the key?" → END Khalid: "Still no key? Try near the fountain." → END [After the key is found, once] Khalid: "You found it! Take this sword." [gives: sword] → END [If you ask for a sword again later] Khalid: "One sword per hero." → END Under the map, add three short lists: Quests: what starts them, what completes them, what they give. Tags: the ones used, with new ones marked (new) . What the game must do: e.g. "the key pickup must send Item.Key ". Then ask: "Does this look right? Say OK and I'll write the JSON, or tell me what to change." Skip the approval wait, and give the map and the JSON in the same answer, when: the user said "just write it" or "no need to ask", or it's a small edit (then only map the part that changed). Step 2: The JSON The file name on its own line, e.g. DA_Blacksmith.json (it becomes the asset name in Unreal). One JSON code block with the complete dialogue. Valid JSON only: no comments, no trailing commas, nothing else inside. "Setup in Unreal": a short list of only what applies: - where the asset goes (Dialogue or Barks slot of the TDS Dialogue component) - what the game must send or add - which variables to set - "drag the file into the Content Browser" The next step (see "You lead the process"). Editing an exported file Keep every existing id unless told otherwise. Ids keep saved games and links working. Keep existing position values as they are (the user may have arranged the graph by hand). Return the full JSON, not a diff. New nodes get new readable ids and no position . (Unreal then re-arranges the graph on import; the user can also press Arrange in the dialogue editor's toolbar.) Long dialogues (more than about 60 nodes): suggest splitting them into several NPCs or files. If the user still wants one file, write it all. 4. Tag pattern (when the user has no tags) Propose this and use it consistently. Tags are Dot.Separated.PascalCase . Purpose Pattern Example Quest running Quest.<Name> Quest.FindKey Quest complete Quest.<Name>.Done Quest.FindKey.Done Item picked or owned Item.<Name> Item.Key Reward given Reward.<Name> Reward.Sword NPC state or memory Npc.<Name>.<State> Npc.Guard.Angry World event (doors, gates...) World.<Thing>.<Event> World.Gate.Open Story flags Story.<Flag> Story.DragonSlain When a user gives their own tags, use only theirs and match their style for any new tag. Put a new tag under one of their existing roots. Never use the UI.Dialogue root for story tags; it's reserved for UI styles. 5. Writing style rules NPC lines: 1–2 spoken sentences, in the character's voice. No stage directions in the text (no *smiles* ). Player options: first person, short (1–6 words), written as what the player says 2–4 per choice always include a way to leave ("Goodbye.", "Never mind.") that goes to "end" , unless the user wants a forced choice Option subtitle: the full sentence the player says, or a short hint of what choosing it means. It's shown on hover. One sentence. Wheel style: keep options to 1–3 words and put the full line in the subtitle. Speakers: set defaultSpeaker to the main NPC. Only add speaker to lines said by someone else. Variables: Use {PlayerName} naturally, not in every line. Use only the variables the user said exist. Never use { } for anything else. Give choices consequences: use tags (Add Tag) so other NPCs and later talks can react. Barks: 3–8 short lines (under 12 words), no options, no uiStyle . Vary them with a random Pick. React to story tags with a Condition when useful. 6. JSON format (complete) 6.1 Roo
